title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fake news article impersonating a real Reserve Bank governor and finance presenter in order to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article never existed but was designed to appear credible enough to deceive investors into trusting a fraudulent service. This deployment bypassed any human editorial review that would have caught the false attribution and checked whether the quoted figures held licenses.

Scammers are using AI to generate convincing fabrications faster than verification systems can debunk them. The report establishes that such impersonation scams have grown significantly, with AI making them harder to distinguish from legitimate content. It is not established how the fake article was distributed, what AI tools created it, or whether the platforms hosting it had systems in place to detect synthetic content.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article claiming Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler never actually occurred. The fabricated piece was designed to promote Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, by using AI to create a convincing false story. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common, with scammers using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to deceive investors.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that investment scams have surged dramatically, with fake investment platforms increasing by 151 percent and phishing scams jumping 279 percent last year. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, along with other politicians and business figures including Alan Kohler, are among the most frequently impersonated people. ASIC warns consumers to verify financial services licenses independently and avoid investments promoted through suspicious online articles and celebrity endorsements, as artificial intelligence is making these scams increasingly difficult to detect.
